title: 22. Interview: Authentication
summary: Interview Q&A for Authentication — 14 questions with model answers.
objectives: Answer 14 Authentication interview questions out loud
Lead with the concept, then a small example, then a tradeoff

sections.title: Conceptual Interview Questions
sections.body:
### Q1. What are the three authentication factors, and why does combining factors of different types matter?
**Answer:** The three classical factors are something you know (password, PIN), something you have (hardware key, OTP app on phone, smartcard), and something you are (fingerprint, face, iris, voice). Multi-factor authentication is only effective when the factors come from different categories, because an attacker has to compromise two independent mechanisms. Two passwords are not MFA — a single phishing site steals both. A password plus an SMS code is weak MFA but still MFA, because stealing the password does not reveal the SMS. The strongest production setups combine a phishing-resistant "have" factor like a FIDO2 hardware key with a "know" or "are" factor, raising attacker cost to the point where wide-scale credential theft becomes uneconomical. The factor type matters more than the factor count.
**Visual:**
```
  KNOW        HAVE        ARE
 password    YubiKey    fingerprint
    |            |           |
    +------+-----+------+----+
           |             |
        2FA (diff types) -- strong
        2 passwords     -- weak (same type)
```

### Q2. Why must password hashes be salted and slow, and what algorithms are appropriate in 2024?
**Answer:** A salt is a per-user random value mixed into the password before hashing, ensuring that two users with the same password produce different hashes and that precomputed rainbow tables are useless. Slowness matters because attackers who steal a hash database mount offline brute-force at the speed of the hash function; fast hashes like MD5 or SHA-1 allow billions of guesses per second on GPUs, while slow KDFs like bcrypt, scrypt, or Argon2id are deliberately designed to be both CPU- and memory-hard, dropping that rate to thousands or fewer per second. Argon2id is the current OWASP recommendation, with bcrypt as a widely-deployed second choice. The cost parameter is tuned so a single verification takes 100–500 ms on production hardware, slow enough to annoy attackers but invisible to real users. PBKDF2 with at least 600,000 iterations is acceptable for legacy systems but inferior to memory-hard options.
**Visual:**
```
password "hunter2"  +  salt (16B random)
        |
        v
   Argon2id (memory=64MB, time=3)
        |
        v
   stored: $argon2id$v=19$m=65536$t=3$p=...$hash
```

### Q3. Why is SMS-based MFA considered weak, and what should replace it?
**Answer:** SMS is delivered over the SS7 telephony signaling protocol, which has known interception vulnerabilities and is reachable by attackers who purchase access on the grey market. SIM-swap attacks — where an attacker convinces a carrier to port a victim's number to a SIM they control — let the attacker receive the victim's OTPs directly, defeating MFA entirely. NIST SP 800-63B deprecated SMS OTP for new deployments in 2016. Replacements include TOTP apps (Google Authenticator, Authy) that compute codes locally from a shared secret, push-based authenticators (Duo, Microsoft Authenticator with number matching) that resist phishing by requiring the user to type a number displayed only on the legitimate login page, and FIDO2/WebAuthn hardware or platform keys that cryptographically bind credentials to the origin domain and are phishing-resistant by construction. The progression is from "thing received over a weak channel" to "thing computed locally" to "thing that cannot be relayed at all."
**Visual:**
```
SMS OTP  ->  TOTP app  ->  Push + match  ->  FIDO2 key
 weak          better         strong          phishing-proof
   |              |              |                 |
 telco attack   local only    number-match     origin-bound
```

### Q4. What is single sign-on (SSO), and what are its benefits and risks?
**Answer:** Single sign-on lets a user authenticate once against a central identity provider (IdP) — Okta, Azure AD, Google Workspace — and then access multiple downstream applications without re-entering credentials, using federation protocols like SAML or OpenID Connect. The benefits are operational: users memorize one strong password instead of fifty weak ones, MFA is enforced centrally, joining and leaving employees are deprovisioned in one place, and security teams get a single audit log for all app access. The risk is concentration: the IdP becomes a single point of failure and a high-value target. When Okta's support case system was breached in October 2023, attackers potentially held keys to federate into 18,000+ customer environments. Mitigations include partitioning IdPs by sensitivity tier, requiring step-up MFA for the IdP itself, hardening the IdP's own support tooling, and maintaining break-glass accounts that bypass SSO for emergency access.
**Visual:**
```
            +------------------+
   user --> |   Identity Prov. |  (SAML / OIDC)
            |   (Okta / AAD)   |
            +--------+---------+
                     |
       +-------------+-------------+
       |             |             |
   App A          App B         App C
   (HR)           (CRM)         (Code)
```

### Q5. How does risk-based or adaptive authentication work, and why is it preferred over blanket MFA for consumer apps?
**Answer:** Adaptive authentication evaluates a risk score on every login using signals like device fingerprint, IP reputation, ASN, geolocation, impossible-travel detection, time of day, and behavioral biometrics such as typing cadence. If the score is low (a returning user on a known device at the usual home ASN), the system allows password-only login to preserve conversion. If the score is high (a new device on a VPN, a login from a country the user has never visited, or a velocity check that flags impossible travel), the system demands step-up MFA, a hardware key, or even blocks the attempt outright. Google's account security works this way — a familiar laptop logs in with just a password, while a brand-new phone on a hotel Wi-Fi is challenged for both an OTP and a hardware key. This is preferred over blanket MFA for consumer apps because every additional friction step measurably drops conversion; risk-based scoring applies friction only where the threat model justifies it.
**Visual:**
```
login attempt
     |
     v
[compute risk: device/IP/geo/velocity]
     |
   +--+--+--------+--------+
  low    medium    high    critical
   |       |        |        |
   v       v        v        v
 allow  step-up  MFA+push  block
```

### Q6. What is passwordless authentication, and what are its trade-offs compared to passwords?
**Answer:** Passwordless authentication replaces the password with a cryptographic credential stored on a hardware or platform authenticator — most commonly a passkey (FIDO2 credential synced across the user's devices via iCloud Keychain or Google Password Manager) or a platform biometric like Windows Hello or Touch ID. On login, the authenticator signs a challenge from the relying party after the user unlocks it with a local biometric or PIN. The credential is never transmitted, is origin-bound (so phishing fails), and cannot be reused across sites. Google reported passkey sign-in success rates 4x higher and 50% faster than passwords. The trade-offs are recovery and portability: if a user loses their only device without a synced backup, they can be permanently locked out; if the sync provider is breached, all synced credentials are at risk. Enterprise deployments mitigate this with admin-managed recovery keys and per-user backup codes, but consumer deployments must invest heavily in recovery UX.
**Visual:**
```
User            Authenticator           Relying Party
 |                  |                       |
 |--unlock biometric|                       |
 |----------------->|                       |
 |                  |<--challenge nonce-----|
 |                  |----signed response--->|
 |                  |                       | verify pubkey
 |<-------OK--------|<----------200---------|
```

### Q7. What is the difference between authentication and authorization, and why do interviewers insist on the distinction?
**Answer:** Authentication answers "who are you?" and verifies identity; authorization answers "what are you allowed to do?" and grants or denies specific actions on specific resources. They are conceptually separate and must be implemented separately because conflating them produces brittle, leaky systems — a service that infers permissions from username ("alice is always an admin") cannot revoke admin without deleting the user, cannot support temporary roles, and cannot survive the user changing their name. The clean pattern is to authenticate once (identity provider issues a token with claims), then authorize per request (a policy engine like OPA, Cedar, or AWS IAM evaluates the claims against the resource and action). Interviewers insist on the distinction because candidates routinely describe authorization mechanisms (RBAC, scopes) when asked about authentication, or describe login flows when asked about access control, revealing a conceptual gap that would cause real bugs in production code.
**Visual:**
```
AUTHN (who?)        AUTHZ (allowed?)
   |                     |
   v                     |
+------+   claims   +----------+
| IdP  | ---------> | Policy   |
+------+            | Engine   |
                    +----------+
                         |
                  allow / deny
```

sections.title: Scenario-Based Interview Questions
sections.body:
### Q1. Your startup's password database was just dumped on a dark-web forum. What do you do in the first hour, and what do you do over the next week?
**Answer:** In the first hour, contain the breach: rotate the database credentials, block the exfiltration path, and force a global password reset for every user. Disable the existing login endpoint and replace it with a reset-password flow that requires email verification. Next, notify affected users transparently — regulators under GDPR and CCPA require notification within 72 hours, and hiding the breach is both illegal and reputationally fatal. Over the next week, conduct a forensic review to determine which hashes were actually exfiltrated, audit the hashing algorithm (if it was bcrypt with cost ≥ 12, the exposure is much less severe than unsalted MD5), and verify that the breach vector (likely SQL injection or a misconfigured backup) is patched. Finally, mandate MFA enrollment at next login for all accounts and add breached-password checking via the HaveIBeenPwned k-anonymity API so any user picking a known-breached password is rejected. The post-mortem should produce engineering tickets for salt rotation, credential stuffing rate limits, and anomaly detection.
**Visual:**
```
hour 1: rotate DB creds -> force global reset -> notify IR team
day 1:  forensic review  -> identify vector    -> patch
week 1: rehash to Argon2 -> enforce MFA        -> breach API check
```

### Q2. A user reports that their account was accessed from a foreign country they have never visited, even though they have a strong password. How do you investigate and prevent recurrence?
**Answer:** First, pull the session audit logs for the affected account and identify the device fingerprint, IP, ASN, user-agent, and exact timestamps of the suspicious access. If the password was not changed, the most likely cause is a credential-stuffing attack — the same password was reused on another site that was breached, and an attacker tried it here successfully. Reset the user's password, revoke all active sessions, and force MFA enrollment. To prevent recurrence, deploy breach-password checking at password-set time (reject any credential appearing in known breach corpora), add device-fingerprint and impossible-travel risk scoring to the login flow, and require step-up MFA when the risk score exceeds a threshold. Long term, migrate the user base toward passkeys or FIDO2 hardware keys so that even a perfectly leaked password cannot be replayed, because the phishing-resistant authenticator will refuse to sign for any non-legitimate origin.
**Visual:**
```
report --> logs --> foreign IP + new device
   --> credential stuffing suspected
   --> reset pw, revoke sessions, enroll MFA
   --> deploy risk scoring + breach API + passkeys
```

### Q3. Your consumer app sees a 30% login conversion drop after you ship MFA. The product team wants to remove it. How do you respond?
**Answer:** First, measure the drop precisely and separate it from concurrent changes — a 30% drop is large enough that something is likely wrong with the UX, not the concept of MFA. Inspect where users abandon: are they dropping at the password step (suggesting a regression), at the MFA enrollment step (suggesting friction), or at the OTP entry step (suggesting deliverability issues with SMS)? Most likely culprits are SMS deliverability, an enrollment flow that demands a phone number up front, or a TOTP setup that exposes the secret as a QR code without a manual-entry fallback. Replace SMS with TOTP or passkeys, defer enrollment to after first login rather than blocking it, and offer "remember this device for 30 days" so returning users skip the second factor. If conversion still drops, switch to risk-based MFA — challenge only new devices or risky geolocations — which preserves 95% of the security benefit at a fraction of the friction. Removing MFA entirely should not be on the table.
**Visual:**
```
30% drop
   |
   v
measure funnel
   |
password | enroll | OTP
   |        |       |
   v        v       v
   UX     defer   TOTP/passkey
                + risk-based
```

### Q4. You are designing authentication for a banking app. Which factors and flows do you choose, and why?
**Answer:** Banking sits at the highest sensitivity tier, so the baseline is mandatory MFA on every login, not just risk-based. The first factor should be a password with strict breached-password rejection and a minimum length rather than complexity rules. The second factor should be a push-based authenticator with number matching (the user must type a number displayed on the login screen into their phone) so that phishing and relay attacks fail; SMS is acceptable only as a fallback for users without smartphones, with a hard deprecation timeline. For high-value transactions — wire transfers above a threshold, adding a new payee, changing the mailing address — require a step-up FIDO2 hardware key or platform biometric, and impose a 24-hour delay before the change takes effect. Sessions should be short (15 minutes idle timeout), tied to the originating device fingerprint, and revoked immediately on logout. Audit logs of every authentication event and every step-up challenge must be retained for years for regulatory compliance under GLBA and PCI DSS.
**Visual:**
```
login:    password + push-with-number-match
view:     15-min session, device-bound
transfer: step-up FIDO2 key + 24h delay
new payee: step-up + 24h delay
```

### Q5. Your company uses Okta for SSO. Okta announces a support-tool breach. What is your incident response?
**Answer:** First, request the exact list of affected support cases from Okta to determine whether your tenant's data was accessed — the breach in October 2023 exposed support case data including HAR files that can contain session tokens. If your tenant is affected, immediately rotate any session tokens or credentials that may have been shared with Okta support, force re-authentication for all active sessions in your downstream apps, and review audit logs for anomalous logins from Okta-federated identities in the breach window. Even if your tenant is not on the published list, treat the announcement as a forcing function: review which of your apps trust Okta as the sole IdP, identify break-glass accounts that bypass SSO, and verify those accounts are secured with hardware keys and stored in a sealed envelope accessible only to a quorum of admins. Long term, partition your IdP strategy — use one IdP for low-sensitivity apps and a separate, more tightly controlled IdP for production infrastructure access — so that a compromise of one does not cascade to all systems.
**Visual:**
```
Okta breach notice
   |
   v
get affected case list --> rotate tokens if exposed
   |
force re-auth all sessions
   |
verify break-glass accounts (quorum + hw key)
   |
long-term: partition IdPs by sensitivity tier
```

### Q6. You are building a CLI tool that authenticates to your SaaS API. Browser-based OAuth is awkward for a CLI. How do you handle it?
**Answer:** The cleanest modern answer is OAuth 2.0 with PKCE and the device authorization grant (RFC 8628), the same flow used by `gcloud`, `gh`, and `aws sso login`. The CLI displays a short user code and a verification URL, opens a browser for the user to authenticate at the IdP, and polls the token endpoint until the user completes authentication or the code expires (typically 15 minutes). The CLI never sees the user's password, the access token is scoped and short-lived, and a refresh token is issued for subsequent silent refresh. PKCE protects against authorization-code interception on the local redirect. As an alternative, you can issue long-lived API tokens for service accounts that cannot perform interactive login, but those should be scoped narrowly, rotated periodically, and stored in the OS keychain (macOS Keychain, Windows Credential Manager, libsecret on Linux) rather than in plaintext config files. Avoid embedding credentials in environment variables that get dumped into shell history or CI logs.
**Visual:**
```
CLI                       IdP
 |---device code request-->|
 |<--user_code + URL--------|
 | show user_code
 | poll /token every 5s    |
                          user opens browser, logs in, enters code
 |<--access + refresh token|
```

### Q7. You discover that 40% of your users reuse the same password across multiple breached sites. What technical and policy changes do you make?
**Answer:** This is a credential-stuffing time bomb — when one of those other sites is breached, attackers will spray the leaked credentials against your login endpoint and a meaningful percentage will succeed. The immediate technical mitigation is to integrate the HaveIBeenPwned k-anonymity API at password-set and password-change time: you send the first 5 characters of the password's SHA-1 hash and receive a list of suffixes that have appeared in known breaches, rejecting any full match. This requires no plaintext disclosure and adds only a few milliseconds of latency. Second, deploy rate limiting per IP and per account — for example, 10 failed attempts per account per 15 minutes triggers a captcha or a temporary lockout — to slow automated stuffing. Third, on next login, require users whose password appears in a breach to reset to a non-breached password, with a clear explanation of why. Fourth, offer and strongly encourage passkey enrollment so the password is no longer the primary factor. Long term, measure credential-stuffing success rates from your audit logs and tune the rate limiter until they approach zero.
**Visual:**
```
40% reuse
   |
   v
HIBP k-anonymity check at set/change
   |
rate-limit per IP + per account
   |
force-reset on next login if breached
   |
promote passkey enrollment
```
